title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
An AI system was used to create a fabricated interview between a real finance presenter and a real central bank official, endorsing a fake cryptocurrency trading platform. The fake article was deployed online without any human verification that the interview had actually occurred or that the endorsement was genuine. This is an impersonation attack, where AI generated content falsely attributed words and positions to real people to lend credibility to a scam.

The failure occurred at the point of deployment. There was no check, human or otherwise, to verify that the interview existed before the article went live. The scammers relied on the polished appearance of AI-generated content and the real names of trusted figures to persuade people to invest in an unlicensed platform. It would have taken basic verification from anyone reviewing the article before publication, such as confirming the interview occurred with the people named.

It is not established whether specific AI tools or services were knowingly designed for this purpose or whether they were repurposed from legitimate uses by the scammers. The incident reflects a pattern reported by Australian financial regulators, but the causes and scope remain under investigation.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
# Summary

A fake online article featured a fabricated interview between ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler and Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock discussing Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The article never actually occurred and was created using artificial intelligence technology. This incident exemplifies a growing category of investment scams that ASIC, Australia's corporate regulator, reports is becoming increasingly common and sophisticated.

ASIC's new research reveals that scammers are building elaborate webs of deception using deepfakes and AI-generated content featuring well-known Australians, including Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, politician Pauline Hanson, and businesswoman Gina Rinehart. Last year, ASIC removed 19,400 scams, a 182 percent increase, including 7,051 fake investment platforms and 5,476 phishing scams. The regulator urges consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through ASIC's public registers before investing and warns that polished content and familiar branding do not guarantee legitimacy.
